1.pericope_label: And in that day seven women shall take hold of one man, saying, We will eat our own bread, and wear our own apparel: only let us be called by thy name, to take away our reproach. In that day shall the branch of the Lord be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the earth shall be excellent and comely for them that are escaped of Israel

schools.summary: Calvin holds that the verse ought not to have been separated from the preceding, the prophet describing the calamity from its effect so that hypocrites may not palliate the warning and hope for an easy escape; he notes that it is inconsistent with the modesty of the sex for a woman to offer herself, that the conditions asked are unreasonable, since the women release the husband from all concern about supplying them with food and request nothing beyond being received within the bond of marriage, and that a wife passing into her husband’s family takes his name and loses her own. On the second verse he grants that the Messianic exposition is plausible in itself, is supported by a later prophet’s words and by the respectful title given to the branch here, and that those who hold it refer the fruit of the earth to Christ’s human nature; but after a careful examination of the whole he does not hesitate to regard both phrases as denoting an unusual and abundant supply of grace to relieve the hungry, the sudden fertility of an exhausted land making the kindness of God the more desirable. Gill rejects the dating in the days of Ahaz, since two hundred thousand women were carried captive at that same slaughter, and refers the verse instead to the wars of the Roman emperors with the Jews, when there were not men enough left for every woman to have a husband; he reports a rabbinic tradition that a conqueror forbade his army to marry another man’s wife but says the time of the prophecy does not agree with it, and on the second verse rejects the readings that make the branch the wise men left among the people or the reforming king, settling with the Targum on the Messiah.

Henry begins from the arithmetic, that providence has ordered nearly equal numbers of males and females to be born on an average of years, while war may leave scarcely one man in seven alive, and observes that as there are deaths peculiar to women in childbirth so there are deaths peculiar to men by the sword in the high places of the field, which perhaps devour more. He lists three reversals of the usual order: men ordinarily make their court to the women, whereas here the women take hold of the men, foolishly fearing as Lot’s daughters did at the ruin of Sodom that in a little time none would be left; women naturally hate to come in as sharers with others, yet seven now consent to become the wives of one; and where the law obliged a husband to provide food and raiment, these women bind themselves to eat bread of their own earning. On the second verse he says the sun breaks out from behind the cloud, takes the branch as one of the prophetical names of Christ, so called because planted by God’s power and flourishing to his praise, and reports that the ancient paraphrase reads it as the Messiah of the Lord.

Clarke complains that the chapter division has interrupted the discourse and broken it off almost in the middle of a sentence, and describes the distress by its adjuncts: the young women, contrary to their natural modesty, become suitors and use pressing importunity, content with a share only of the rights of marriage in common with several others, renouncing the legal demands of a wife on her husband and begging only the name and credit of wedlock and freedom from the reproach of celibacy, for which he quotes a Roman woman’s plea in a poem for the empty name of marriage and a husband’s name upon her tomb. He reports a Jewish commentator’s dating in the days of Ahaz, when a hundred and twenty thousand men were slain in a day and the widows were said to be multiplied beyond the sand of the sea, and notes that the opening words are omitted in the Septuagint and in manuscripts. On the second verse he takes the branch as an appropriate title of the Messiah, with the Chaldee and a Jewish commentator behind him, and reads the fruit of the land as the great person to spring from the house of Judah, or as the blessings consequent on his redemption. Wesley makes the seven a certain number for an uncertain, notes that virginity was esteemed a reproach since children were an honour to parents and a blessing of God, especially among a people from some of whose loins the Messiah was to spring, takes the branch for the Messiah, and reads the fertility of the land as one mercy including all temporal blessings together with the spiritual and eternal.

Ellicott calls the chapter division wrong and makes the verse the climax of the chastisement of the daughters of Zion and the companion picture to an earlier scene, since as men there sought a protector eagerly and in vain, so women here seek a husband, those who had been wooed and courted and were proudly fastidious now supplicating in eager rivalry, the seven to one implying a land depopulated by war and so making polygamy natural, and that not on the usual conditions of having food and clothing found for them but as working for their own livelihood. He would read the last clause as an imperative, take thou away, and identifies the reproach as childlessness, which from the Jewish standpoint was not only the great sorrow but the great shame of womanhood, implying a sin of which men thought it the chastisement. On the second verse he calls this the first distinct prophecy in the book of a personal Messiah, notes that the thought of the branch though not the word recurs later and that the word itself is found in two later prophets who probably inherited both from this passage, adds that the appearance of the Branch has the restoration of outward fertility as its accompaniment, and dismisses as missing the true meaning the interpretation that takes the branch collectively for vegetation and so nearly synonymous with the fruits of the earth. Keil and Delitzsch treat the verse as closing the threat against the women of Jerusalem, a side-piece to the threat against the national rulers and part of a judgment whose centre and focus is Jerusalem, where the ungodly glory ripe for judgment was concentrated and where the light of the true and final glory would concentrate itself; the judgment, they say, was itself the medium of salvation, since when Jerusalem was judged it would be sifted, and by being sifted rescued, pardoned and glorified.

debates: Where does the chapter begin? Clarke, Ellicott and Calvin all object that the division separates this verse from what precedes and breaks the discourse mid-sentence.

When is the scene set? Gill refers it to the wars of the Roman emperors and rejects the days of Ahaz, since women were carried captive in that same slaughter; Clarke reports the Ahaz dating without deciding.

Is the branch a person or a crop? Ellicott calls it the first distinct prophecy of a personal Messiah and dismisses the vegetation reading; Henry, Gill, Clarke and Wesley all take it of Christ; Calvin, having weighed the Messianic case, makes both branch and fruit denote an abundant supply of grace.
outliers: Clarke quotes a Roman woman’s plea in a poem for the empty name of marriage and a husband’s name upon her tomb.
Henry compares the women’s fear to that of Lot’s daughters at the ruin of Sodom, who thought it reached further than it did.
Keil and Delitzsch hold that the judgment was itself the medium of salvation, since a city judged would be sifted, and by being sifted rescued.

3.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass, that he that is left in Zion, and he that remaineth in Jerusalem, shall be called holy, even every one that is written among the living in Jerusalem: when the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and shall have purged the blood of Jerusalem from the midst thereof by the spirit of judgment, and by the spirit of burning

schools.summary: Gill finds in the third verse the doctrine of the final perseverance of the saints, with their sanctification and election secured in the clauses that follow, and takes those left in Zion for the Gospel church, who abide by the truths and ordinances and persevere to the end when the floor is purged of its chaff. On the fourth verse he takes Zion for the church in general and her daughters for particular churches, and the filth for false doctrine of every kind, which will be removed in the latter times of the Gospel dispensation. Calvin objects as too limited to the reading that those written in the book of life shall be holy, and would keep the two clauses separate, such repetition being frequent among the Hebrews when the same gift of God is set out under various titles; he warns that the promise cannot be applied to the external church, into which many are admitted under the name of believers who have nothing answering to their profession and who exceed the small number of the good as chaff exceeds wheat in the barn. On the fourth verse he turns the argument against a common assumption, since it is generally believed that the calamities which reduce the church do her grievous injury, whereas this is the very method by which God washes away her filth; he reads the blood as covering not murders only but defilements of every description, calls the two clauses a reduplication saying the same thing twice, and draws the practical fruit, that our spots are washed away by chastisement and that where abounding iniquity goes unpunished we are corrupted along with others, so that God must warn us in earnest and, like a physician, apply the medicine and the lancet. He adds that the purification is the work of the Spirit, who takes his names here from the effects he produces, so that wherever such phrases occur one may as well say by the truth, by the power, by the righteousness of the Spirit.

Clarke keeps the register administrative, taking it for the enrolment in which a citizen’s name stands, and notes that numbering and registering the people was agreeable to the law of Moses and probably always practised, being useful and even necessary in sound policy, though the king’s design in numbering was of another kind, to enrol men for his army. On the spirit of burning he takes it for the fire of God’s wrath, gathering the people into a furnace to separate the dross from the silver, and cites one prophet who sets the same out with great boldness of imagery, God threatening to gather them into the midst of the city as into a furnace and blow the fire upon them, and another who shows him sitting as a refiner and purifier of silver; the whole, he says, alludes to a chemist purifying metals, who first judges the state of the adulterated ore, then kindles the proper degree of fire and applies the requisite test, and so parts the precious from the vile. Wesley says those left shall be really holy, reads the blood as blood-guiltiness, and takes the two names of the Spirit from his effects, judgment because he executes it in the church and in the consciences of men, separating the precious from the vile and convincing men of sin, and burning because he consumes the dross in the church and in the heart and inflames the souls of believers with love to God; he adds that the burning stands opposed to the older legal purification, which was by water.

Keil and Delitzsch put the weight of the third verse on the word holy, since where formerly people in that city had been distinguished by rank and condition without regard to moral worth, holy would now become the one chief title of honour and would belong to every individual, the national calling of Israel being realized in the persons of all; they note that shall be called is not simply equivalent to shall be but presupposes it, and that the term denotes what is withdrawn or separated from the world. On the fourth verse they match the double purification to the two scenes of judgment in the previous chapter, take the filth of the daughters for the moral pollution hidden under their vain and coquettish finery, and render the second phrase spirit of sifting rather than of burning. Ellicott draws the same contrast historically, the prophet turning from the city that then was, with its hypocrisies and crimes and harlot fashions, to a new one realizing the ideal of two psalms, where everyone should be called holy and the name should be no unreal mockery but should express the self-consecration and purity of the inhabitants. He takes the next phrase literally as for life and identifies it with the book or register of life in which are written the names of those worthy of living in the heavenly city, concluding from an examination of the places where it occurs that while the image involves the idea of an election it excludes that of an irreversible predestination, the election having to be made sure by a life in harmony with it. On the fourth verse he makes the link back to the daughters of Zion explicit and distinguishes the two evils by their remedies, since the uncleanness beneath their outward show of beauty could be washed away as with a baptism of repentance, whereas the blood of Jerusalem, ranging from murders to the sacrifices in which the women had borne a conspicuous part, needed the fiery baptism of the wrath of God; he prefers the more literal sense of breath or blast for spirit, and notes that the word rendered burning is used elsewhere for destruction generally.

debates: What does the book of the living imply? Ellicott holds that while it involves an election it excludes an irreversible predestination, the election having to be made sure by a corresponding life; Gill finds in the same verse the final perseverance of the saints; Calvin keeps the clauses separate and warns that the promise does not cover the external church.

Are the two purifications the same? Keil and Delitzsch match them to the two scenes of judgment in the previous chapter and render the second spirit of sifting; Ellicott distinguishes the filth that can be washed from the blood that needs a fiery baptism; Calvin treats the pair as a reduplication saying one thing twice.

What is the spirit of burning? Clarke makes it the fire of God’s wrath refining metal; Wesley makes it the Holy Spirit consuming dross and kindling love, opposed to the old purification by water; Calvin says the Spirit simply takes his name from the effect he produces.
outliers: Clarke compares the whole to a chemist who judges the state of the adulterated ore, kindles the proper degree of fire, applies the test, and parts the precious from the vile.
Calvin argues that calamities which reduce the church do not injure her but are the method by which God washes her, and compares the physic and the lancet.
Keil and Delitzsch note that shall be called is not simply equivalent to shall be, but presupposes it.
themes: holy as the one title of honour
a spirit named from its effect

5.pericope_label: And the Lord will create upon every dwelling place of mount Zion, and upon her assemblies, a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night: for upon all the glory shall be a defence. And there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge, and for a covert from storm and from rain

schools.summary: Calvin sums the fifth verse up in a sentence, that there will not be a corner of Mount Zion on which the grace of God does not shine, and glosses the second noun as the place where men assemble rather than a proclamation. He explains the allusion to the exodus as customary with the prophets, who recall that deliverance whenever they describe a remarkable blessing, since God then made a display of the boundless treasures of his grace; what chiefly deserved commemorating was that the cloud protected the people from excessive heat by day while the fire went before them by night to keep them from straying. He is careful that the promise not be pressed literally, since the return from captivity would be no less striking than the going out of Egypt without a cloud and a fire, God displaying his grace by other methods not less remarkable, much as one might say today that he will enlighten us by his Spirit and give tongues of fire to spread the Gospel through the world. On the last verse he refuses to promise exemption, since believers remain exposed to many calamities and when they escape one danger they meet another, but holds the protection of the Lord to be of itself sufficient against every inconvenience; good and bad alike suffer, he adds, but the bad have no refuge and must be utterly overwhelmed, whereas the godly, enduring heat and cold, have a safe retreat, provided the glory spoken of earlier shines in them, for it is by carrying God’s mark that a man may rest assured of protection when the tempest comes. Gill takes each dwelling place for a particular church in Gospel times, the word signifying a place well fitted up, established and settled, and identifies the tabernacle of the last verse with Christ, who tabernacled in our nature.

Clarke works the text itself, reporting a manuscript and two versions that read he shall bring rather than create, on the ground that the cloud already exists and the Lord will bring it over; four manuscripts omit the word all before dwelling place, rightly as it seems to him, since the station was the mountain itself and no other; the same word stands before assemblies in the versions, having probably only changed its place by mistake; and twenty-five manuscripts and twenty-two editions give assemblies in the plural. He blames a connecting mark in the last clause, which joins two words that ought not to be joined and has thrown obscurity over the sentence and misled most translators, and takes the cloud and smoke for a manifest allusion to the pillar and to the glory that rested on the tabernacle, comparing another prophet’s promise to be a wall of fire round about and a glory in the midst. On the last verse he supplies the object from travel, since in countries subject to violent tempests as well as intolerable heat a portable tent is a necessary part of a traveller’s baggage, and such tents are met with throughout the region. Wesley glosses the verb as producing in a marvellous manner, as it were by a new creation, takes the cloud for a pillar like that which directed the people out of Egypt and so an assurance that God would be their protector and their glory, and reads the last verse as saying that the Lord himself shall be the tabernacle.

Ellicott notes that the verb create carries all the solemn force it has in the opening sentence of the law and is one of this prophet’s favourite words, and that the noun rendered dwelling-place is almost always used of the tabernacle or temple, which settles what the assemblies are: not meetings of the people for counsel or debate, as in a Greek city, but their solemn gatherings in the courts of the temple. He finds the last clause of the fifth verse almost startlingly abrupt and reads it as an overarching canopy of divine love stretched over the glory of the new Jerusalem, noting that the word for defence is still used by Jews of the canopy held over bride and bridegroom at a wedding and that the covering set over the altar of an Italian church probably represents the image before the prophet’s mind. On the last verse he says that in the manifested glory men would find what a traveller finds in his tent, protection against every form of danger, against the scorching heat of noon and against the pelting storm. Keil and Delitzsch read the cloud against the older deliverance and mark what has changed, since God once guided and shielded the people with a smoke-cloud by day and a fire-cloud by night, which either moved before them like a pillar or floated above them as a roof, whereas the Israel of the final redemption would no longer need the pillar, its wanderings being over, but only the cloudy covering, which God creates, the verb always denoting a divine and miraculous production. On the last verse they settle the grammar first, refusing to make the miraculous roofing the subject, since the words disagree in gender and it would make no sense to say that a canopy is a booth, and prefer to take Zion as the subject, so that the city becomes a booth, a place of security and concealment.

debates: What is the cloud for? Keil and Delitzsch say the redeemed no longer need a pillar to lead them, their wanderings being over, but only a covering; Calvin uses the exodus as a customary figure and warns against pressing it literally; Clarke and Wesley keep the allusion to the pillar itself.

What are the assemblies? Ellicott insists they are solemn gatherings in the temple courts, not meetings for counsel as in a Greek city; Calvin glosses the word as the place where men assemble rather than a proclamation; Clarke reports manuscripts that give the word in the plural.

Who or what is the tabernacle of the last verse? Keil and Delitzsch make Zion itself the subject, the city becoming a booth; Gill makes it Christ, and Wesley the Lord himself; Clarke and Ellicott keep it a traveller’s tent.
outliers: Ellicott notes that the word for defence is still used by Jews of the canopy held over bride and bridegroom at a wedding, and compares the covering over the altar of an Italian church.
Clarke blames a connecting mark in the last clause of the fifth verse for joining two words that ought not to be joined and misleading most translators.
Calvin refuses to promise exemption from calamity, holding that good and bad alike suffer but that only the godly have a refuge.
themes: a verb kept for divine acts
a city that becomes a booth
